questions.subject: OS
questions.question: In Round Robin scheduling, what happens when time quantum is too small?

options.text: Response time improves but context switch overhead increases

questions.explanation: Smaller quantum gives better responsiveness but frequent context switching increases overhead.
questions.shortcut: RR trade-off: smaller q => better response, higher switching overhead.

questions.subject: OS
questions.question: Page size is 4 KB, virtual address space is 32-bit. How many bits are used for offset?
questions.explanation: 4 KB = 2^12 bytes, so offset needs 12 bits.
questions.shortcut: Offset bits = log2(page size in bytes).

questions.subject: OS
questions.question: A process creates 3 children. Each child creates 2 children. Total number of processes including parent?
questions.shortcut: Total = 1 + n + n*m for this pattern.

questions.subject: OS
questions.question: A Round Robin scheduler uses time quantum = 10 ms with 50 ready processes. Save time is 2 us and restore time is 3 us per switch. What is the context-switch overhead percentage over one full cycle?
questions.explanation: Context-switch time = 2 + 3 = 5 us. One full cycle CPU time = 50 x 10,000 us = 500,000 us. Total context-switch overhead per cycle = 50 x 5 = 250 us. Percentage = (250 / 500,000) x 100 = 0.05%.
questions.shortcut: For small switch time vs quantum: overhead% ~= (context switch time / quantum) x 100.
questions.commonMistakes: Forgetting save+restore both count, or incorrect 10 ms to 10,000 us conversion.

questions.subject: OS
questions.question: Which statements are true for kernel-level threads?

options.text: The kernel maintains TCBs for kernel threads.
Switching between threads in the same process is typically faster than process switching.
Blocking is per-thread, so one blocked thread need not block all peer threads.
The OS scheduler treats kernel threads as independently schedulable entities.

questions.explanation: All four statements are advantages/properties of kernel-level threads: OS-visible scheduling entities with per-thread blocking and generally cheaper same-address-space switches than full process switches.
questions.shortcut: Kernel threads are OS-known and schedulable independently; blocking is per-thread.
questions.commonMistakes: Confusing kernel-level behavior with user-level thread limitations.
